article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Reinforcement learning extends the adaptivity axis through learned instructional policies
description: The chapter presents reinforcement learning as replacing hand-authored control logic with policies "learned from experience rather than explicitly programmed." An RL agent observes the learning environment state, selects an instructional action, receives a reward signal, and gradually develops strategies maximizing cumulative reward. For serious games, RL reframes instructional adaptation as sequential decision-making covering task sequencing, difficulty calibration, intervention timing, and scaffolding fading, operating at interaction timescales for genuinely real-time adaptivity.
requirements: Effective RL-based instructional adaptation requires external systems providing cognitive state inference and carefully designed reward functions to optimize pedagogically meaningful objectives
constraints: RL optimizes observables, not cognitive states: it does not inherently address what the learner knows, misunderstands, or needs to develop conceptually
There is no agreed methodology for specifying pedagogically valid reward functions for complex skill domains
target_learners: Learners in serious games requiring real-time instructional adaptation
target_learning_goals: Task sequencing, difficulty calibration, intervention timing, and scaffolding fading optimized from interaction data
examples: RL actions include deciding when to provide hints versus allowing productive struggle, described as the educationally beneficial experience of working through a challenge without immediate assistance
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

citation: Wenqian Xu, Feng Ji. (2026). Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09305
title: Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model (RLMM)
description: The RLMM is a psychometric measurement framework for sequential process data that treats a person's inverse-temperature parameter βj as an ability to choose higher-valued actions under a Boltzmann policy. It replaces the MDP-MM's person-specific tabular value functions with "a shared parametric action-value function Qθ(s,a)", using centered and globally normalized advantages, a soft Bellman-consistency penalty encoding known task dynamics, and a block-coordinate MAP estimation procedure. It also yields step-level influence diagnostics that identify behaviorally critical decisions.
requirements: Known task dynamics (transition and reward structure) used in the soft Bellman-consistency penalty
Identification constraints: state-wise centering and global normalization of the advantage function to remove softmax translation and co-scaling freedom
constraints: Uses a single positive ability parameter, which the authors note cannot fully capture strategy selection, task persistence, and exploration patterns
In open-ended environments, estimates depend on how researchers define states, actions, and rewards
target_learning_goals: measuring latent decision-making ability from action-sequence process data
examples: Applied to peg-solitaire simulations with known true abilities and to AQUALAB gameplay logs from the Open Game Data export
key_sources: Wenqian Xu, Feng Ji. (2026). Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09305

article_title: Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised
citation: Singh, N. P., Wang, X., Garikipati, A., Ciobanu, M., Mao, Q., & Das, R. (2026). Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised Fine-Tuning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06385
title: RL-SFT-RL: a multi-stage pipeline combining pedagogically aligned RL, difficulty-weighted SFT on RL-generated synthetic data, and an optional second RL round
description: The article proposes a three-phase training framework formalized in Algorithm 1: an initial RL stage (DAPO with asymmetric clipping) that identifies and trains on the base model's hard negatives; an SFT phase that uses the RL-trained model to synthesize training data, filtered and weighted by difficulty; and an optional second RL round reusing the Phase 1 hard dataset. The authors describe "a virtuous cycle of improvement" in which each stage builds on the previous one, and state the pipeline "comprising the initial RL stage for hard-negative identification, the difficulty-weighted SFT phase for knowledge distillation, and the optional final RL refinement" is formalized in Algorithm 1.
requirements: A base model with a benchmark (here CDPK) usable to identify failure modes via repeated attempts, plus a reward model trained to prioritize pedagogically sound responses that guide learners rather than simply providing answers
constraints: The third RL stage is optional; the article reports primary results only on teacher-exam-style multiple-choice questions from CDPK
target_learners: developers of educational AI tutors for classroom and platform integration
target_learning_goals: cross-domain pedagogical knowledge (strategic teaching capacity distinct from content knowledge)
examples: The pipeline transformed Qwen3-32B into EduQwen 32B-RL1 (94.13%), EduQwen 32B-SFT (96.20%), and EduQwen 32B-SFT-RL2 (96.52%) on the CDPK Benchmark
key_sources: Singh, N. P., Wang, X., Garikipati, A., Ciobanu, M., Mao, Q., & Das, R. (2026). Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised Fine-Tuning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06385

citation: Crone Eveline A., Wendelken Carter, van Leijenhorst Linda, Honomichl Ryan D., Christoff Kalina, Bunge Silvia A. (2009). Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning. Developmental Science, 12(1), 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2008.00743.x
title: Relational integration account of rostrolateral prefrontal cortex function
description: The article endorses the account that RLPFC is specifically engaged when multiple relations must be jointly considered, whereas DLPFC is sensitive to task difficulty factors such as working memory and response selection rather than relational complexity per se. In adults, "RLPFC did not differentiate between REL-0 and REL-1 trials (REL-2 > REL-0, REL-1), whereas DLPFC exhibited an increase from REL-0 to REL-1 and from REL-1 to REL-2." The developmental findings extend this account: children recruit RLPFC for both 1st- and 2nd-order relational processing, and the adult specialization for integration is still undergoing change between ages 8 and 12.
requirements: Performance of problems that require joint consideration of multiple relations to detect RLPFC's selective engagement
constraints: The article notes alternative theoretical accounts of RLPFC involvement exist and are not adjudicated here
The account rests on cross-sectional age-group comparison rather than longitudinal within-person change
examples: Adults in the RPM-like task showed RLPFC activation selectively for REL-2 problems, replicating Christoff et al. (2001), while children engaged RLPFC for REL-1 as well as REL-2 problems
key_sources: Crone Eveline A., Wendelken Carter, van Leijenhorst Linda, Honomichl Ryan D., Christoff Kalina, Bunge Silvia A. (2009). Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning. Developmental Science, 12(1), 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2008.00743.x

article_title: Social learning through prediction error in the brain
citation: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2
title: Reinforcement learning via reward prediction error as a framework for social learning
description: The review's organizing framework is reinforcement learning, in which an agent compares expected reward to actual reward and uses the discrepancy — the reward prediction error — to update value functions and policy. It argues that "Prediction-based computational principles in the brain may be strikingly conserved between self-referenced and other-referenced information", so that other-referenced (vicarious) prediction errors can mediate social learning under the same computational principles as self-referenced learning.
requirements: A reward signal, a value function, and a policy through which the agent computes expected value and updates behavior
constraints: Vicarious reinforcement in an RL framework would have to be model-based, since it is unclear how a model-free RL system could learn about another agent without modeling its potential thoughts and future actions
target_learners: humans and nonhuman animals learning from observation
target_learning_goals: learning about others' actions and reward outcomes through observation
examples: Temporal difference learning applied to observational learning of another person's stimulus-reward contingencies in the modified Q-learning studies discussed
key_sources: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2

article_title: Deciding for others diminishes model-based decision-making but depends on individual prosociality
citation: Yangchu Huang, Xinyi Du & Shanshan Zhen. (2026). Deciding for others diminishes model-based decision-making but depends on individual prosociality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00397-0
title: Reinforcement learning drift-diffusion modelling as a framework for decomposing prosocial decision-making into latent cognitive computations
description: The reinforcement learning drift-diffusion model (RLDDM) formalises value-based decisions as evidence accumulation processes in which noisy evidence favouring one option accumulates until it hits a decision boundary. Per the article, "The strength of RLDDM is its ability to identify the specific cognitive computation affected by an experimental effect of interest". In this study it decomposed self-other differences into model-based weights, model-free weights, model-free learning rates, stickiness parameters, decision boundary and non-decision time, disentangling mechanisms that choices alone cannot separate.
requirements: Choices and response times must both be recorded so the drift-diffusion process can be fitted jointly
Task structure must be learnable so model-based and model-free value estimates can be computed separately
constraints: The article notes the dual-system distinction may not capture the full spectrum of strategies, and the eligibility trace decay parameter showed relatively poor parameter recovery, so λ was fixed at 1
target_learning_goals: understanding reinforcement learning (model-based vs model-free) in value-based decision-making
examples: Applied to a 92-participant two-step task, the RLDDM isolated reduced model-based weights, a slower model-free learning rate, and shorter non-decision time for others
key_sources: Yangchu Huang, Xinyi Du & Shanshan Zhen. (2026). Deciding for others diminishes model-based decision-making but depends on individual prosociality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00397-0

article_title: Teaching tools in evidence based practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about meta-analysis.
citation: Bath-Hextall Fiona, Wharrad Heather, Leonardi-Bee Jo. (2011). Teaching tools in Evidence Based Practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about Meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3123313/
title: Use RLOs as a supplement to, not a replacement for, other delivery approaches such as lectures
description: The article recommends that meta-analysis RLOs be used alongside didactic lectures rather than instead of them. The feedback showed that "the RLOs supported learning but students still valued the lectures therefore we recommend that RLOs are used as a supplement but not to replace other delivery approaches". Some students reported needing lecturer support, while others wanted the RLO before the lecture as a basic introduction.
requirements: RLOs are integrated into a course alongside the usual lecture on the topic
constraints: Some students would have struggled with the content using the RLO alone as a replacement for the didactic lecture
target_learners: healthcare students on postgraduate nursing and public health courses
target_learning_goals: understanding meta-analysis concepts within evidence based practice
examples: Students received their usual lecture on meta-analysis and were then given time to work through the two RLOs in a computer lab
key_sources: Bath-Hextall Fiona, Wharrad Heather, Leonardi-Bee Jo. (2011). Teaching tools in Evidence Based Practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about Meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3123313/

article_title: Teaching tools in evidence based practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about meta-analysis.
citation: Bath-Hextall Fiona, Wharrad Heather, Leonardi-Bee Jo. (2011). Teaching tools in Evidence Based Practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about Meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3123313/
title: RLO development process: storyboard, dual peer review, packaging and release
description: The article describes a quality-controlled development process for RLOs based on a well established methodology. Storyboards (written templates of proposed content) were developed through an iterative development cycle, sent to experts for peer review prior to development, and after a prototype was built the RLOs went through "a second internal peer review by experts and evaluation by students" before packaging and release.
requirements: Academic experts review storyboards for accuracy and appropriateness using a structured proforma
Second peer review assessing usability and appropriateness of media before release
target_learners: healthcare students who will use the resulting RLOs
target_learning_goals: accurate, usable e-learning resources for difficult statistical concepts
examples: Figure 1 shows the stages beginning with team meetings to scope content and ideas for analogies and media
key_sources: Bath-Hextall Fiona, Wharrad Heather, Leonardi-Bee Jo. (2011). Teaching tools in Evidence Based Practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about Meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3123313/

article_title: Research Learning Communities: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Dr Jo Rose, Professor Sally Thomas, Dr Lei Zhang, Dr Anna Edwards, Dr Andres Augero, Ms Pooneh Roney. (2017). Research Learning Communities: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Research Learning Communities intervention with Evidence Champions and cross-school workshops
description: Research Learning Communities is a school-improvement intervention in which two Evidence Champion teachers per school attend four one-day workshops per year with peers from up to four other schools, examining research on an agreed focus such as literacy or growth mindsets. Champions then "develop, apply and evaluate school or key-stage wide improvement strategies using the learning from the workshops" and support colleagues. Workshops follow a cycle from identifying good practice and developing a research question through trialling approaches to analysing impact data, with year two workshops led by the Champions themselves.
requirements: Evidence Champions need to be able to commit to the full duration of the intervention, attend all the workshops, and have time in school to develop their ideas and discuss the project with their colleagues
at least one Evidence Champion came from the senior leadership team
constraints: Staff turnover was a barrier to implementation because Champion roles were intended to be held by the same people throughout
not all evidence champions were able to attend every workshop
target_learners: primary school pupils in Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: teachers' awareness, understanding and use of educational research
pupil attainment in reading, numeracy and grammar, punctuation and spelling
examples: 60 treatment schools worked across 14 RLCs, each comprising Evidence Champions from up to five schools, with workshops held in participating schools
key_sources: Dr Jo Rose, Professor Sally Thomas, Dr Lei Zhang, Dr Anna Edwards, Dr Andres Augero, Ms Pooneh Roney. (2017). Research Learning Communities: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581267

article_title: A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education.
citation: Almomani Emad, Tobin John, Fernandes Sonia, Sullivan Jacqueline, Saadeh Omar, Mustafa Emad, Pattison Natalie, Alinier Guillaume. (2025). A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education. BMC Medical Education, 25:1434. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07765-9
title: Reflective Learning Conversation (RLC) debriefing model
description: The RLC model is a co-designed, progressive, multimodal, learner-centered post-simulation debriefing framework for interprofessional groups with varied seniority and experience in multicultural environments. The article states it is "informed by Bloom's Taxonomy, Appreciative Inquiry, and Plus/Delta methods" and is "explicitly co-designed to promote gradual cognitive development" while mitigating cognitive overload through incremental reflection and scaffolding over multiple simulations. It was co-designed by an 18-member working group of doctors, nurses, researchers, educators, and patient representatives.
requirements: ALS instructors require hands-on practice workshop and online training on the RLC debriefing sheet and its delivery format before use
constraints: Tested in face-to-face simulation debriefing; applicability to AI, AR, and VR simulation contexts is untested
Incremental questioning risks rigidity if not adapted to learners' needs
target_learners: Interprofessional healthcare providers of varying seniority and clinical experience in multicultural learning groups
examples: Used as the experimental debriefing condition across 12 simulation and debriefing sessions per participant in ERC ALS courses, compared against Norris and Bullock debriefing.
key_sources: Almomani Emad, Tobin John, Fernandes Sonia, Sullivan Jacqueline, Saadeh Omar, Mustafa Emad, Pattison Natalie, Alinier Guillaume. (2025). A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education. BMC Medical Education, 25:1434. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07765-9

article_title: A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education.
citation: Almomani Emad, Tobin John, Fernandes Sonia, Sullivan Jacqueline, Saadeh Omar, Mustafa Emad, Pattison Natalie, Alinier Guillaume. (2025). A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education. BMC Medical Education, 25:1434. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07765-9
title: CREST, LCJR, and CTR observation tools with high interrater reliability
description: Three validated rubric tools were used for real-time observation of team-leader performance: the Clinical Reasoning Evaluation in Simulation Tool (CREST), the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR), and the Critical Thinking Rubric (CTR). Twelve ALS faculty members assessed interrater reliability, "revealing high levels of agreement": CREST α = 0.968, ICC = 0.972; LCJR α = 0.953, ICC = 0.959; CTR α = 0.853, ICC = 0.859. The same faculty member rated each participant on all three tools during the same observation period.
requirements: Faculty must be trained in scoring each tool; ratings are completed immediately after each observed scenario to minimise observer bias
constraints: The article notes these tools "mainly capture observable behaviours and may not reflect participants' internal reasoning or metacognitive processes"
target_learners: Healthcare professionals acting as team leaders in ALS simulation scenarios
examples: Applied at three time points (beginning, midpoint, end of the two-day course) whenever each participant held the designated team leader role.
key_sources: Almomani Emad, Tobin John, Fernandes Sonia, Sullivan Jacqueline, Saadeh Omar, Mustafa Emad, Pattison Natalie, Alinier Guillaume. (2025).
